source_hint: Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, Mathematics for Machine Learning (Ch. 5, Vector Calculus).
rationale: Differential calculus — derivatives, gradients, the chain rule — is needed to derive and train gradient-based ML models.
uncertainty: Some curricula fold calculus inside optimization, so this could double-count the existing calculus -> optimization -> machine-learning path rather than add a distinct dependency.
note: Direct calculus->ML prerequisite; complements the existing calculus->optimization and optimization->ML edges in /data.

source_hint: Boyd & Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization (Appendix A, linear-algebra background).
rationale: Continuous optimization is expressed over vectors and matrices; quadratic forms, norms, and eigenstructure from linear algebra underpin gradient and Newton methods.
uncertainty: Elementary optimization can be taught with single-variable calculus alone, so linear algebra may be a co-requisite rather than a strict prerequisite.

source_hint: Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Ch. 1-2).
rationale: Probabilistic modeling, likelihoods, and reasoning about generalization in ML are stated in the language of probability theory.
uncertainty: ML often reaches learners via statistics rather than probability theory directly, so this could overlap the existing probability-theory -> statistics -> machine-learning path.

source_hint: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis (Ch. 1).
rationale: Bayesian inference is an application of probability theory; priors, likelihoods, and posteriors are probability-theoretic objects.
uncertainty: If 'probability theory' is read as measure-theoretic foundations, most applied Bayesian work needs far less, overstating the prerequisite depth.
note: /data already has probability-distribution->BI and random-variable->BI; this adds the subfield-level dependency.

source_hint: Ross, A First Course in Probability (Ch. 4-5).
rationale: A probability distribution is defined as the law of a random variable, so the random-variable concept is usually introduced first.
uncertainty: Distributions can be taught before/independently of random variables (e.g. as mass/density functions), so the direction is pedagogy-specific; could be adjacent_to.

source_hint: Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, Mathematics for Machine Learning (Ch. 5 & 7).
rationale: Gradient descent is defined by the gradient, a calculus construct; derivatives are needed to grasp the update rule and convergence behavior.
uncertainty: A learner can apply gradient descent mechanically from given formulae without calculus, so it may be a conceptual rather than strict prerequisite.

rationale: Statistical inference assumes data are drawn from probability distributions; the distribution concept precedes estimation and testing.
uncertainty: Introductory descriptive statistics needs no formal distribution theory, so the prerequisite applies mainly to inferential statistics.

source_hint: Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, Mathematics for Machine Learning (Preface).
rationale: Machine learning rests broadly on mathematics (linear algebra, calculus, probability); a mathematics foundation precedes the field.
uncertainty: This is very high-altitude and largely subsumed by the specific subfield prerequisites already present, so it may add little and could be dropped as redundant.

source_hint: Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, Mathematics for Machine Learning (Ch. 2-3).
rationale: Gradient descent operates on vectors and inner-product geometry; linear-algebra fluency helps reason about step directions and conditioning.
uncertainty: Scalar gradient descent needs no linear algebra, so this is helpful-but-not-required and might be better modeled as adjacent_to.

source_hint: Ross, A First Course in Probability (Ch. 4).
rationale: A probability distribution models/represents the stochastic behavior (the law) of a random variable.
uncertainty: The pair is tightly definitional; reviewers may prefer prerequisite_for or adjacent_to, and the direction could be argued either way.

source_hint: Editorial; cf. /data, which places field:statistics directly under formal_sciences rather than under mathematics.
rationale: Statistics and mathematics are deeply intertwined, but statistics is conventionally a distinct discipline; adjacent_to records the strong link without asserting containment.
uncertainty: Some taxonomies treat statistics as part_of mathematics; choosing adjacent_to over part_of is a deliberate, contestable call.
note: Deliberately NOT proposed as part_of; see report.md.

source_hint: Editorial; 'math for ML' curricula commonly pair the two (e.g. Mathematics for Machine Learning, Parts I-II).
rationale: Linear algebra and calculus are the two core continuous-mathematics pillars for ML and are typically learned in parallel.
uncertainty: adjacent_to here is a weak placeholder; there is no strong directional dependency and QC may prefer no edge at all.
